title: Karna looks at the sun
hook: Karna strings the bow, one sentence stops him, and he looks up at Surya, the father he doesn't know
carry: surya, the sun, sees what the arena can't

segments.voice: Yesterday at Draupadi's swayamvara: the stiff bow, and kings thrown to the floor. Your line: ahamkara, the ego, is what falls.

As the kings give up, one by one, a man rises whom we've met before. Karna. Found in a basket on the river, raised by a charioteer, born with armor on his body. The bow has just thrown kings to the floor in front of everyone. Karna walks up to it.
screen: `THE KINGS GIVE UP.` → `KARNA RISES.` → `HE WALKS TO THE BOW.`

segments.voice: In the version Ganguli translated, Karna lifts the bow and strings it. He fits the arrows. He's about to shoot. And Draupadi speaks, loudly, so the whole arena hears. In paraphrase: I will not choose a suta for my husband. A suta: a charioteer, a charioteer's son. Karna laughs, a bitter laugh, the text says. He glances up at the sun, and puts the bow down. Readers hear Draupadi's line in different ways: holding the contest to the terms her brother read out, which counted birth; guarding her father's hope for Arjuna; or the old sting of birth used against a man who could clearly do the thing. The poem doesn't settle it. But stay with the glance. The sun, as we know and the arena doesn't, is Karna's father: Surya, the sun god. And for Hindus the sun isn't only a star. In the Rig Veda, Surya is the eye of the gods, the one who sees everything. Hindus still greet him every morning: pouring water toward the rising sun, an offering called arghya, or bowing to him in Surya namaskar. Later in this poem, Karna himself is a devoted worshipper of the sun. So here's what this moment holds. The arena looks at Karna and sees a charioteer's son. Surya, who sees everything, sees his own son. And Karna looks up to him at the moment he's turned away, without knowing whose face he's looking for. Karna and Draupadi will meet again in another hall, later in this serial. For now the bow is back on the ground, and the arena waits for someone else.
screen: `I WILL NOT CHOOSE A SUTA.` · `HIS FATHER IS THE SUN.` · `SURYA, THE EYE OF THE GODS.` · then, large: `SURYA SEES WHAT THE ARENA CAN'T.`

segments.voice: If you can, face a window or the morning light. Many Hindus greet the sun at dawn by pouring a little water toward it, arghya, and saying Om suryaya namah, I bow to the sun. If you have water, hold a cup and do the same, and if you pray, add one thing you wish someone could see in you. If you don't pray, just feel the light on your face for a few breaths. It shines on you no matter what anyone calls you.
Draupadi's swayamvara. Today, Karna at the bow, one sentence from the princess, and a glance at the sun.
Your line: Surya, the sun, sees what the arena can't. Karna looked up to a father he didn't know. That's day seven hundred forty-two.

howItsDone: Many Hindus offer water to the rising sun each morning, called arghya, and in Bihar and eastern Uttar Pradesh the festival of Chhath is given to Surya; Karna's story is retold in storytelling, theater, dance and novels.

Karna.meaning: Kunti's firstborn son by the sun, raised by a charioteer

suta.meaning: a charioteer, or a charioteer's son

Radheya.meaning: son of Radha, a name for Karna

arghya.meaning: water offered to the rising sun

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Swayamvara Parva (Karna strings the bow; Draupadi refuses a suta; Karna glances at the sun and puts the bow down)

notes: All paraphrase, including Draupadi's sentence. Confirm in Ganguli that Karna strings the bow, that Draupadi's refusal comes before he shoots, and that he laughs bitterly, glances at the sun and throws the bow aside.

Scholar check: the Pune Critical Edition is reported to omit Karna's attempt and Draupadi's refusal. The script says 'in the version Ganguli translated' and makes no claim about other manuscripts; a Keeper should decide whether to say more.
Week end (days 736–742): the hook looks back over the week. It assumes day 736 is set in the lac house.
The readings of Draupadi's line are unattributed and given without ranking; this is a sensitive moment about birth and caste, and the Keeper should check the framing.
'Karna and Draupadi will meet again in another hall' points ahead to the dice game without telling it.
